packs.title: Visitor choices and public park pages
packs.promise: Read offered exhibits, a visitor garden and farm, then make records from actual public park paths.

q.s: Separate what you can see from what an offered label supplies.
st: Enter the opened visitor galleries and choose three objects you can study comfortably without touching, copying or photographing them.
For each, remember one visible material or construction relationship. Use a plain observation rather than assigning a cultural, spiritual or personal meaning.

Read the object’s offered label and paraphrase one fact it explicitly supplies. Keep the label-derived fact beside, and separate from, your own observation; choose a different object if a suitable label is absent.
Write three paired observation/label records after exit if needed. Add one sentence explaining how a label changed a first impression, without claiming to speak for its maker or community.

q.t: Two silos and a new page
q.s: Make a three-panel record from a public view of adapted silos.
st: Find an opened public footpath view outside the playground from which the two adapted silos are actually visible. Keep the path and nearby entries clear.
Make two simple original outline notes of visible silo forms, then paraphrase the City’s farming-history connection. Do not copy a City photo, plan or public artwork.
On your own paper or device, make a three-panel personal page: one observed silhouette, one relationship between the two forms, and one imagined future reuse clearly marked as your idea.
Revise the middle panel so its relationship is specific to the pair you can actually see. Add a caption separating your observation, sourced history and imagined reuse.

q.t: An open field path and return
q.s: Follow one bounded public park path and record its turn.
st: Reach the opened eastern public concrete path and choose the recorded field-side return only if the whole short segment is open and comfortable. Arrange arrival and departure independently.
Walk calmly along the path toward its northern field-side bend. Notice two actual changes in the relationship between the paved route and grass fields; do not enter a field or use a facility.

Turn at that bend and retrace the same public path. End sooner and use another day if a closure or uncomfortable condition prevents the intended short return; never improvise through a preserve or playground.
Write two path/field observations and one difference in what you noticed on the return. Use distance as desk planning, with no speed target or claim to a full park loop.

packs.title: Old Town rooms and street records
packs.promise: Connect public library and gallery visits with distinct Old Town exteriors and a short square return.

q.s: Collect the ways an opened branch helps a visitor find a next step.
st: Enter the actually opened branch and choose ordinary public wayfinding scope, excluding the Teen Corner, staff areas, booked rooms and occupied workstations.
Collect three actual direction records: a public-area label, a shelf or service category, and a visible relationship between two public areas. Choose another lawful public clue if a type is absent.
For each, write what it helps a visitor distinguish without copying a book cover, screen, patron record or a long sign. Do not treat a public service label as permission to use that service.
Write one possible next step for your own visit, based on a clue you found. Keep it optional; there is no borrowing or staff-service task.

q.t: A hotel and a personal postcard
q.s: Write a street-view postcard with observation and imagination kept apart.
st: Find an opened lawful public sidewalk view of the actual hotel facade, keeping its entrances and guest circulation clear. Do not enter to improve the view.
Notice two actual facade relationships, such as an opening within a wall or a repeated form along the frontage. Write plain observations without recording guests or copying a sign.

Write a personal three-sentence postcard: one observed relationship, one sourced 1923 opening note, and one imagined visitor moment clearly marked as your imagination. It is your writing, not a former guest’s account.
Revise the first sentence with a second actual detail so the postcard belongs to this exterior. Keep it on your own paper or device; no sending or leaving it at the hotel is required.

q.s: Retrace one named pedestrian path before the next street.
st: Reach the opened southern named public square path and confirm that its short Walnut-side segment is comfortable and outside event fences, private patios and queues.
Walk calmly along the public paving-stone path toward its northern end before Walnut. Notice two actual changes in how adjoining frontage and public pavement meet.
Turn before the Walnut street crossing and retrace the same short public segment. Leave the next street and any private event outside the movement record.
Write a completed-return note, two actual frontage/pavement observations and one comparison between the outward and return views. Do not describe a full square circuit or district walk.
